questions.skill: Design and use a simulation to estimate the probability of a compound event
questions.prompt: A player makes 60% of her free throws, and each shot is independent of the others. Describe how to use random digits 0 to 9 to simulate one trial of 2 free throws.
questions.prompt_markup:
A player makes 60% of her free throws, and each shot is independent of the others.
Describe how to use random digits 0 to 9 to simulate one trial of 2 free throws.
questions.correct_answer: Let the digits 0 to 5 stand for a make and 6 to 9 stand for a miss. Choose 2 random digits; each pair of digits is one trial.
questions.grading_note: Any plan where 6 of the 10 digits stand for a make, and each trial uses 2 digits, is correct.

questions.skill: Design and use a simulation to estimate the probability of a compound event
questions.prompt: A player makes 60% of her free throws; each shot is independent. In the simulation, the digits 0 to 5 mean a make and 6 to 9 mean a miss. Each pair of digits is one trial of 2 shots: 32  70  15  86  41  09  55  63  27  84 In how many trials are both shots made? Estimate the probability that both shots are made.

sections.skill: Use a simulation to decide whether a difference between treatments is significant

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Use a simulation to decide whether a difference between treatments is significant
questions.standard_level: High school (Common Core high-school standard; this bank places it at Grade 9 as a second forward step. This is an instructional choice, not an official grade assignment.)
questions.prompt: In an experiment, 40 similar plants were randomly assigned: 20 got a new plant food (Group A) and 20 got none (Group B). Group A grew a mean of 12 cm and Group B a mean of 9 cm. The data were re-randomized 100 times to simulate no treatment effect; a difference of 3 cm or more happened 2 times. Is there evidence that the plant food made a difference? Explain.
questions.prompt_markup:
In an experiment, 40 similar plants were randomly assigned: 20 got a new plant food (Group A) and 20 got none (Group B). Group A grew a mean of 12 cm and Group B a mean of 9 cm. The data were re-randomized 100 times to simulate no treatment effect; a difference of 3 cm or more happened 2 times.
Is there evidence that the plant food made a difference? Explain.
questions.correct_answer: Yes. With random assignment, a difference that large happened by chance only about 2% of the time, so the results give evidence of a treatment effect (but do not prove it).

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Use a simulation to decide whether a difference between treatments is significant
questions.standard_level: High school (Common Core high-school standard; this bank places it at Grade 9 as a second forward step. This is an instructional choice, not an official grade assignment.)
questions.prompt: In the same kind of randomized experiment (plants randomly assigned to plant food or none), the data were re-randomized 100 times to simulate no treatment effect. A difference of 3 cm or more happened 40 times. What does this suggest about the plant food?
questions.prompt_markup:
In the same kind of randomized experiment (plants randomly assigned to plant food or none), the data were re-randomized 100 times to simulate no treatment effect. A difference of 3 cm or more happened 40 times.
What does this suggest about the plant food?
questions.correct_answer: The difference could easily be due to chance, so the experiment does not give evidence that the plant food made a difference.
